WRT 205 · State of AI · May 2026

The Amplifier

Why artificial intelligence doesn't replace human potential; it multiplies it. An opinion essay on the state of AI in April 2026.

By Kyle Jansen  ·  Syracuse University

scroll

Introduction

The divide isn't who uses AI. It's who uses it well.

Argument I: Creative Amplification Argument II: Democratization Argument III: Real-World Impact

Last semester, I watched a complete brand diagnostic tool get built in real time: a full working website with a user interface, questionnaire system, data analysis layer, and customized growth report, produced in the time it would have taken a traditional development team to schedule their first meeting. The tool was built using Manus, a Singapore-based AI execution engine valued at roughly $2 billion, and the raw material it worked from was thirty years of brand strategy expertise from my father, a consultant who has worked with companies like Coca-Cola and Home Depot. Neither the AI nor my father could have done it alone, and that is precisely the point; together, they built something neither could have imagined creating independently.

That moment changed how I think about artificial intelligence, and I want to be clear that I am not someone who came to this opinion from a distance. As a Division I student-athlete at Syracuse, time is my most limited resource, and balancing practices, lifts, travel, and a full course load would be genuinely overwhelming without AI helping me study, summarize, and prepare. I use AI the way a serious athlete uses a strength coach: not to do the work for me, but to make every hour of work count more. I have watched it transform confusing concepts into clear, step-by-step explanations, used it to research and organize this very essay, and seen it build a real business tool from scratch during my internship, all in a single semester.

And I have heard the fear. That AI will take jobs, hollow out critical thinking, poison the environment, and hand the future to machines. I take those concerns seriously; some of them are real. But after everything I have witnessed this semester, in this class and in the field, my opinion is clear: AI is the most powerful amplifier our generation has ever had access to, and the people who learn to use it well will define what comes next. The real divide in the future won't be between people who use AI and those who don't. It will be between those who use it well and those who don't.

"The real divide won't be between people who use AI and those who don't; it will be between those who use it well and those who don't."

To understand why I believe this, we need to understand what AI actually is, and more importantly, what it has recently become.

What is AI, and why does the distinction between types matter?

Artificial intelligence is, at its core, software that learns patterns from data and uses those patterns to make decisions or generate outputs. For most of recent history, AI meant generative AI, tools like ChatGPT that respond to prompts with text, images, or code. Useful? Absolutely. Transformative? Increasingly. But the real shift happening right now is the emergence of what researchers call agentic AI: systems that don't just respond to requests but actively plan, execute, and complete multi-step tasks with minimal human supervision. As my classmates Chloe Mitchell and Sophia Quezada noted in their presentation, agentic AI can "plan and execute multi-step processes, use tools and APIs to complete tasks, and operate proactively with minimal human input," a fundamentally different relationship between human and machine than the chatbot model most people picture (Mitchell and Quezada, WRT 205 course website). This distinction matters enormously for the arguments I am about to make.

Argument I

AI accelerates human creativity. It doesn't replace it.

The most persistent misconception about AI is that it is a substitute for human thought, but my experience, and the evidence, points to the opposite. When used with intention, AI removes the friction between what humans know and what they can create, allowing people to operate at a level that would have been impossible working alone.

The Manus demonstration I ran this semester is the clearest example I have. Watch what this tool actually does:

Watch on YouTube

Manus AI: Full Software Demonstration

youtu.be/3fTv_uXr5oQ  →

What you are watching is not AI replacing a developer; it is AI executing on a human's expertise. My father spent thirty years developing a "growth agenda" methodology for brand consultancy, working with some of the largest consumer companies in the world, and when we fed that framework into Manus, it didn't invent the strategy; it translated it into a fully deployable, functional tool. The intelligence was entirely his, shaped over decades of real-world experience. The execution was AI's, completed in hours rather than months. The result was something that combined the depth of one with the speed of the other, and that combination is exactly what makes agentic AI so significant for anyone with expertise worth building on.

This is precisely the distinction that a recent McKinsey analysis identifies as the real source of AI value. While most companies have rushed to use AI for basic productivity, automating tasks, cutting costs, and speeding up existing workflows, McKinsey argues that the genuine competitive advantage lies in business model reinvention: using AI to create entirely new offerings, reshape economics, and build things that were previously impossible. Early productivity gains matter, but they erode as adoption spreads. What endures is the advantage built by those who used AI not just to do existing work faster, but to do work that couldn't be done before (Montard et al.).

"The future belongs to organizations that use AI to amplify human judgment."

Mautner and Tota, WRT 205 course website

Understanding why Manus represents something meaningfully new requires understanding the difference between generative and agentic AI. Generative AI, as CleverDev Software explains, "creates content when prompted"; it is reactive and response-based, answering questions and drafting text on demand. Agentic AI, by contrast, "can plan and carry out complex tasks across multiple platforms to achieve specific objectives" without step-by-step human instruction (CleverDev Software), and that makes it something categorically different from the chatbot model most people picture when they think of AI. Manus is agentic, meaning it doesn't just answer questions; it builds things, iterates on them, and delivers a finished product, and that shift from conversational partner to execution engine is what makes the creative amplification argument not just plausible, but proven.

I also feel this personally as a student, and it is worth being specific about what that looks like. AI has transformed how I study, not by doing my thinking for me, but by removing the bottlenecks that used to slow my thinking down; when a concept doesn't click, I don't stay stuck for an hour trying to decipher a textbook, I use AI to get a different explanation, a better analogy, or a clearer breakdown until it connects. The learning still happens in my head, but I get there faster, and for a Division I athlete managing 20-hour practice weeks, film sessions, travel, and a full academic schedule, that kind of efficiency is not a convenience. It is genuinely how I stay competitive in the classroom while fully committing to my sport.

Argument II

AI is leveling the playing field for small businesses and individuals.

For most of business history, the gap between large corporations and small operators was partly a gap in resources, but just as significantly a gap in access: access to sophisticated marketing analysis, access to around-the-clock customer service, access to custom software, data analytics, and professional-grade creative work. Large enterprises had entire departments dedicated to capabilities that small business owners had to either go without entirely or pay steep fees to outsource on a project-by-project basis.

AI is collapsing that gap with remarkable speed, and the data is beginning to confirm what people on the ground are already experiencing.

A groundbreaking JPMorgan Chase Institute report published in April 2026, drawing on transaction data from 4.6 million businesses, found that small business AI adoption has spread faster than any comparable technology in modern history, outpacing the diffusion rates of electricity, personal computers, and the internet. The report tracks actual payments to AI services, not self-reported intentions, making it one of the most objective measures of adoption behavior available. While gaps remain, as employer firms outpace solo operators and knowledge-intensive industries move faster than labor-intensive ones, the trajectory is clear: AI is reaching small businesses, and it is doing so quickly.

Heather Kasten, President and CEO of the Greater Sarasota Chamber of Commerce, put it plainly in a March 2026 column: "What once required an entire department can now be accomplished with the right tools and a willingness to adapt." She describes AI as "redefining what's possible for businesses of every size," not replacing people, but empowering them to "spend less time on repetitive tasks and more time focused on strategy, relationships and growth" (Kasten). That framing resonates with what I saw in my father's consultancy. He didn't need a development team, a UX designer, and a data analyst to build his diagnostic tool. He needed Manus and thirty years of expertise.

Mautner and Tota, WRT 205 course website

The democratization argument also extends beyond business. From what I have seen among my peers, almost every student around me uses AI in some form, whether they admit it or not. My friends use it to create study guides, check their work, and simplify difficult readings. A classmate who struggles with a subject and previously had no access to a private tutor now has something functionally close to one, available at any hour. The same personalization and accessibility that AI is bringing to small business is arriving in classrooms, and as my classmates Janice and Katelyn noted in their presentation on AI in education, the core benefits are personalization, efficiency, and accessibility (Janice and Katelyn, WRT 205 course website). For students who don't have the resources to pay for supplemental tutoring or academic support services, that is not a minor benefit. It is a genuine equalizer.

Argument III

AI is solving problems that humans couldn't crack alone.

The first two arguments could theoretically apply to many technologies. The third is what makes AI genuinely historic: it is beginning to solve problems at a scale and speed that exceeds what human intelligence, operating alone, could realistically achieve.

Consider breast cancer screening. Breast cancer is the most common cancer for women globally, and despite decades of medical advances, roughly one in five screenings still fails to detect cancer that is present, a false negative rate that has stubbornly resisted improvement. In March 2026, Google published results from the largest NHS study ever conducted on AI in mammography, covering 175,000 women across twelve clinical sites. The findings were definitive: AI detected 25% of the interval cancers that human radiologists missed, identified more invasive cancers overall, produced fewer false positives, and reduced the time specialists spent reading scans by nearly a third; crucially, it achieved all of this without access to patient histories, working only from the mammogram images themselves (Google Health, 2026).

The same story is playing out in drug discovery. Developing a new medicine typically takes ten to twelve years and costs over $2.5 billion, with a staggering 90% failure rate in clinical trials. Writing for the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026, a Novartis researcher described how AI-driven simulations allowed their team to systematically test thousands of gene candidates for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, a process that "could have been prohibitively slow without AI" but with it rapidly identified several dozen viable targets for wet-lab testing (World Economic Forum). AI is not inventing drugs; it is compressing the timeline and reducing the failure rate of the humans who do.

"AI can strengthen individualized instruction, find patterns teachers miss, and benefit neurodiverse learners and students with IEPs, creating possibilities that were previously unavailable."

Mitchell and Quezada, WRT 205 course website. Source: U.S. Department of Education, 2023.

The pattern is consistent across domains. In education, the U.S. Department of Education's 2023 report emphasized that AI's greatest potential lies in personalization and accessibility, reaching students whose learning needs have historically gone unmet by standardized instruction. In environmental science, as my classmates Tony S. and Taylor D. noted in their presentation, AI's capacity to optimize smart grids, improve renewable energy forecasting, and reduce fuel waste in transportation represents a meaningful counterweight to the energy costs of AI infrastructure itself; I will address that point directly in a moment (Tony S. and Taylor D., WRT 205 course website).

Addressing the Concerns

The fears are real. But they are not the whole story.

I want to be honest about what the critics get right, because the optimistic case is stronger when it doesn't pretend there are no costs.

The environmental concern is legitimate. Researchers Shaolei Ren and Adam Wierman, writing in the Harvard Business Review, documented that training a single large AI model can consume thousands of megawatt-hours of electricity and emit hundreds of tons of carbon, with data centers demanding enormous quantities of freshwater for cooling. These are real costs, and they fall disproportionately on communities near the data centers, not on the people most benefiting from the technology (Ren and Wierman). I take this seriously, but as Tony S. and Taylor D.'s presentation showed, AI is simultaneously being deployed to solve the very environmental problems its infrastructure creates; it is optimizing energy grids, improving renewable forecasting, and reducing transportation waste, which means the conversation is not as simple as AI being purely harmful to the environment.

From Class: Ayden Hagemann & Hailey Wong, "AI & the Brain"

"Relying on AI for instant answers can reduce active problem-solving and critical thinking, weakening neural pathways and potentially leading to mental passivity and diminished intellectual engagement."

Hagemann and Wong, WRT 205 course website. Source: Liz Mineo.

The cognitive concern is also worth taking seriously. My classmates Ayden Hagemann and Hailey Wong presented compelling research suggesting that excessive AI reliance can weaken independent reasoning, what researchers call cognitive offloading, and Matthew Treadwell's presentation cited an MIT study finding lower brain electrical connectivity in ChatGPT-using groups compared to those writing without AI assistance (Treadwell, WRT 205 course website). I don't dismiss this. The distinction that matters, and that I try to practice, is between using AI as a tutor, to understand something better, versus using it as a shortcut, to avoid understanding it at all; the tool isn't the problem, the relationship with the tool is, and that is a distinction every student and professional should be thinking carefully about.

And the job displacement fear? The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation analyzed the actual employment data from 2024 and found something the headlines largely ignored: AI generated over 8,900 direct jobs in AI development and operations, and the data center construction boom it created produced more than 110,000 construction jobs in a single year. An MIT analysis cited in the same report found that only 11.7% of the labor market could even theoretically be automated under current AI capabilities; history consistently shows that automation reallocates work rather than eliminating it, just as the printing press didn't end writing, and the spreadsheet didn't end accounting. AI will not end human work; it will change what that work looks like, and the people positioned to thrive will be the ones who learned to work alongside it rather than resist it.

Conclusion

The amplifier generation

I started this essay watching AI build a complete business tool from thirty years of human expertise, and I want to end it somewhere more personal, because the stakes of this conversation are not abstract for me.

I am a Division I athlete and a full-time student at Syracuse. I have roughly the same number of hours in my week as everyone else, and fewer unobligated ones. For students in my position, and for the first-generation student who can't afford a tutor, the small business owner who can't afford a development team, and the radiologist working through 5,000 scans a week with a global shortage of colleagues, AI is not an abstraction. It is a real and immediate expansion of what is possible.

The McKinsey analysis I cited earlier makes a point I keep returning to: the companies that failed to capture value from AI were the ones that used it only to do existing work faster, while the ones that built lasting advantage were the ones that used it to do things that couldn't be done before. I think that's true for individuals too; the students who will benefit most from AI won't be the ones who use it to skip the thinking, but the ones who use it to think at a higher level than they ever could working alone, pushing themselves further than their own cognitive limits would otherwise allow.

"AI is not about replacing people. It's about empowering them."

My classmates spent this semester examining AI from every angle, covering its effects on the brain, its role in education, its environmental footprint, its political implications, and its business potential. What strikes me looking across all of those presentations is that the underlying question in every one of them is the same: are we in charge of this, or is it in charge of us? I think the answer is still ours to determine. But the window for making that choice intentionally is narrowing.

AI is the amplifier. The question is what you are going to amplify.
